e-12591.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a Point
e-12591.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t) = \langle t, -2t, t^2 \rangle$ at the point where $t = 1.$
e-12591.worked_solution:
To compute the curvature $\kappa (t),$ we will use the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t),$ $\mathbf r'(1),$ and $\|\mathbf r'(1)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,-2,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find $\mathbf r''(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2),2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,2⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{{3}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12608.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a General Point
e-12608.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2, \: 2t, \: 1 \right\rangle$, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature of this curve as a function of $t.$
e-12608.worked_solution:
The curvature $\kappa (t)$ is given by

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3} .
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4({t}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative $\mathbf{r}''(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩=⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,2,0⟩\times ⟨2,0,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2t & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{4}{8({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}=\frac{1}{2({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12592.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve
e-12592.problem: Using the cross product formula for curvature, find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t) = \langle 2t, 1+t^2\rangle$ as a function of $t.$
e-12592.worked_solution:
To compute the curvature $\kappa (t),$ we will use the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩=⟨0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2,\,2t,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2t & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 2t \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \| = 4,
$$

and therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{4}{{(2\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}})}^{3}}=\frac{1}{2{(1+{t}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{t}^{3},\,2t⟩$ for $t\ge 0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,0,0).$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t},\,{t}^{3},\,2t⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}=1 \\ {t}^{3}=0 \\ 2t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨1,0,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}2)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,6t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨1,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =2j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{5})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a Point
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{t}^{3},\,2t⟩$ for $t\ge 0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,0,0).$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t},\,{t}^{3},\,2t⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}=1 \\ {t}^{3}=0 \\ 2t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨1,0,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}2)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,6t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨1,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =2j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{5})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩$ for $t\ge 0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,0,0).$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t=1 \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0-{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,{e}^{-0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0-{e}^{-0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-2{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,-2{e}^{-0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,0⟩⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i-2k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a Point
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩$ for $t\ge 0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,0,0).$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t=1 \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0-{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,{e}^{-0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0-{e}^{-0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-2{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,-2{e}^{-0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,0⟩⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i-2k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ for $t>0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(2,1,0).$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩ & =⟨2,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2t=2 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4i+2j+4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4+16} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{3}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to the point P(2,1,0) on the given curve. We know that

r(t)=⟨2,1,0⟩⟨2t,t2,ln⁡t⟩=⟨2,1,0⟩.

Equating the respective components gives

{2t=2t2=1ln⁡t=0.

From the first equality, t=1. This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, P(2,1,0) is at the tip of r(1).

Now, we calculate r′(t), r′(1), and ‖r′(1)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(2t),ddt(t2),ddt(ln⁡t)⟩=⟨2,2t,1t⟩r′(1)=⟨2,2,1⟩‖r′(1)‖=22+22+12=3

Next, we find r″(t) and r″(1):

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a Point
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ for $t>0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(2,1,0).$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩ & =⟨2,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2t=2 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4i+2j+4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4+16} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{3}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}=1 \\ {e}^{-t}=1 \\ 2t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},-{e}^{-0},2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},{e}^{-0},0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i+2j+2k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}

$$

Question 5
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨3sin⁡t,3cos⁡t,4t⟩ for 0≤t<2π, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point P(0,−3,4π).

a
35
b
23
c
325
d
13
e
29
Submit

decision.explanation: The point corresponds to t=π. Then r'(π)=⟨-3,0,4⟩ and r''(π)=⟨0,3,0⟩. Their cross product is ⟨-12,0,-9⟩, with magnitude 15, while ‖r'(π)‖=5. Thus κ(π)=15/5³=3/25.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩$ for $0\le t<2\pi ,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(0,-3,4\pi ).$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩ \\ ⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩ & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-3 \\ 4t=4\pi .\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=\pi .$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ is at the tip of $r(\pi ).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-12i-9k \\  & =3(-4i-3k) \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =3\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =3(5) \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{15}{{5}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to the point P(0,−3,4π) on the given curve. We know that r(t)=⟨0,−3,4π⟩⟨3sin⁡t,3cos⁡t,4t⟩=⟨0,−3,4π⟩.

Equating the respective components gives {3sin⁡t=03cos⁡t=−34t=4π.

From the third equality, t=π. This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, P(0,−3,4π) is at the tip of r(π).

Now, we calculate r′(t), r′(π), and ‖r′(π)‖: r′(t)=⟨ddt(3sin⁡t),ddt(3cos⁡t),ddt(4t)⟩=⟨3cos⁡t,−3sin⁡t,4⟩r′(π)=⟨3cos⁡π,−3sin⁡π,4⟩=⟨−3,0,4⟩‖r′(π)‖=(−3)2+02+42=25=5

Next, we find r″(t) and r″(π): r″(t)=⟨ddt(3cos⁡t),ddt(−3sin⁡t),ddt(4)⟩=⟨−3sin⁡t,−3cos⁡t,0⟩r″(π)=⟨−3sin⁡π,−3cos⁡π,0⟩=⟨0,3,0⟩

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude: r′(π)×r″(π)=|ijk−304030|=|0430|i−|−3400|j+|−3003|k=−12i−9k=3(−4i−3k)‖r′(π)×r″(π)‖=3(−4)2+02+(−3)2=316+9=3(5)=15

Therefore, the curvature at t=π is κ(π)=‖r′(π)×r″(π)‖‖r′(π)‖3=1553=352=325.

$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-12i-9k \\  & =3(-4i-3k) \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =3\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =3(5) \\  & =15\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t33,22t2,t⟩, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature of this curve as a function of t.

Hint: You can use the fact that r′(t)×r″(t)=−2i+2tj−2t2k.

a
2
b
2(t2+1)3
c
1(t2+1)2
d
2(t2+1)2
e
2t2+1
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨t²,√2t,1⟩, so ‖r'(t)‖=√(t⁴+2t²+1)=t²+1. The given cross product has magnitude √(2+4t²+2t⁴)=√2(t²+1). Therefore κ(t)=√2(t²+1)/(t²+1)³=√2/(t²+1)².

Question 6
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t33,22t2,t⟩, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature of this curve as a function of t.

Hint: You can use the fact that r′(t)×r″(t)=−2i+2tj−2t2k.

a
2
b
2(t2+1)3
c
1(t2+1)2
d
2(t2+1)2
e
2t2+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t33),ddt(22t2),ddt(t)⟩=⟨t2,2t,1⟩‖r′(t)‖=(t2)2+(2t)2+(1)2=t4+2t2+1=(t2+1)2=t2+1

Notice that t2+1>0 for any real value t.

Since we are told that

r′(t)×r″(t)=−2i+2tj−2t2k,

we have

‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=(−2)2+(2t)2+(−2t2)2=2+4t2+2t4=2(t2+1)2=2(t2+1).

Therefore, the curvature is

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=2(t2+1)(t2+1)3=2(t2+1)2.

Given the curve r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of t.

a

b
 2
c
12
d
 25
e
 12(t2+1)3/2
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨-sin t,-sin t,√2 cos t⟩ has magnitude √2. Also r''(t)=⟨-cos t,-cos t,-√2 sin t⟩, giving r'(t)×r''(t)=⟨√2,-√2,0⟩ with magnitude 2. Thus κ(t)=2/(√2)³=1/√2 for all t.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}\,\,
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}|k \\  & =\sqrt{2}i-\sqrt{2}j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2+2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

a
 2(t2+1)3/2
b
 2
c
12
d
 25
e
 12(t2+1)3/2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by:

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(cos⁡t),ddt(cos⁡t),ddt(2sin⁡t)⟩=⟨−sin⁡t,−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩‖r′(t)‖=(−sin⁡t)2+(−sin⁡t)2+(2cos⁡t)2=sin2⁡t+sin2⁡t+2cos2⁡t=2

Next, we find the second derivative r″(t):

r″(t)=⟨ddt(−sin⁡t),ddt(−sin⁡t),ddt(2cos⁡t)⟩=⟨−cos⁡t,−cos⁡t,−2sin⁡t⟩

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

r′(t)×r″(t)=⟨−sin⁡t,−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩×⟨−cos⁡t,−cos⁡t,−2sin⁡t⟩=|ijk−sin⁡t−sin⁡t2cos⁡t−cos⁡t−cos⁡t−2sin⁡t|=|−sin⁡t2cos⁡t−cos⁡t−2sin⁡t|i−|−sin⁡t2cos⁡t−cos⁡t−2sin⁡t|j+|−sin⁡t−sin⁡t−cos⁡t−cos⁡t|k=2i−2j

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=(2)2+(−2)2=2+2=2 Therefore, the curvature is:

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=2(2)3=12

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}\,\,
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}|k \\  & =\sqrt{2}i-\sqrt{2}j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2+2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨−t,4,1+sin⁡t⟩ for 0≤t≤π, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of t.

a
1sin2⁡(t)
b
1
c
sin⁡t(1+cos2⁡(t))3/2
d
cos⁡t(1+cos2⁡(t))3/2
e
sin⁡t1+cos2⁡(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨-1,0,cos t⟩ and r''(t)=⟨0,0,-sin t⟩, so their cross product is ⟨0,-sin t,0⟩. Its magnitude is sin t because sin t≥0 on [0,π]. Since ‖r'(t)‖=√(1+cos²t), κ(t)=sin t/(1+cos²t)^(3/2).

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨-t,\,4,\,1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $0\le t\le \pi $, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-1,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-1,0,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t\ge 0$ when $0\le t\le \pi .$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t))^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨−t,4,1+sin⁡t⟩ for 0≤t≤π, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of t.

a
1sin2⁡(t)
b
1
c
sin⁡t(1+cos2⁡(t))3/2
d
cos⁡t(1+cos2⁡(t))3/2
e
sin⁡t1+cos2⁡(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖: r′(t)=⟨ddt(−t),ddt(4),ddt(1+sin⁡t)⟩=⟨−1,0,cos⁡t⟩‖r′(t)‖=(−1)2+02+(cos⁡t)2=1+cos2⁡(t)

Next, we find the second derivative r″(t): r″(t)=⟨ddt(−1),ddt(0),ddt(cos⁡t)⟩=⟨0,0,−sin⁡t⟩

Now, we compute the cross-product:

r′(t)×r″(t)=⟨−1,0,cos⁡t⟩×⟨0,0,−sin⁡t⟩=|ijk−10cos⁡t00−sin⁡t|=|0cos⁡t0−sin⁡t|i−|−1cos⁡t0−sin⁡t|j+|−1000|k=−sin⁡tj

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=|sin⁡t|=sin⁡t Notice that sin⁡t≥0 when 0≤t≤π.

Therefore, the curvature is

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=sin⁡t(1+cos2⁡(t))3/2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a General Point
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨-t,\,4,\,1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $0\le t\le \pi $, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-1,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-1,0,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t\ge 0$ when $0\le t\le \pi .$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t))^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2,2t2,2t⟩, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature of this curve as a function of t.

Hint: You can use the fact that r′(t)×r″(t)=−8i+4j.

a
12t
b
5(t2+1)3
c
2(5t2+1)3/2
d
2(5t2+1)3
e
52(5t2+1)3/2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t2),ddt(2t2),ddt(2t)⟩=⟨2t,4t,2⟩‖r′(t)‖=(2t)2+(4t)2+(2)2=4t2+16t2+4=4(5t2+1)=25t2+1

Since we are told that

r′(t)×r″(t)=−8i+4j,

we have

‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=(−8)2+42=64+16=80=45.

Therefore, the curvature is κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=45(25t2+1)3=458(5t2+1)3=52(5t2+1)3/2.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms that ‖r'(t)‖=2√(5t²+1) and ‖r'(t)×r''(t)‖=4√5. Hence κ(t)=4√5/[2√(5t²+1)]³=√5/[2(5t²+1)^(3/2)], confirming option e.

Given the curve r(t)=⟨3,3t,t3⟩ for t>0, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of t.

a
3t4(1+t4)3/2
b
1(1+t4)3/2
c
t1+t4
d
231+t4
e
2t3(1+t4)3/2
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨0,3,3t²⟩ and r''(t)=⟨0,0,6t⟩. Their cross product is ⟨18t,0,0⟩, with magnitude 18t since t>0. Also ‖r'(t)‖=3√(1+t⁴). Thus κ(t)=18t/[27(1+t⁴)^(3/2)]=2t/[3(1+t⁴)^(3/2)].

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨3,\,3t,\,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t>0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩=⟨0,\,3,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(3)^{2}+(3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{9(1+{t}^{4})} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨0,\,3,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\times ⟨0,\,0,\,6t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 6t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =18t\,i\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =|18t|=18t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$
Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{18t}{{(3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}})}^{3}}=\frac{2t}{3(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

Given the curve r(t)=⟨3,3t,t3⟩ for t>0, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of t.

a
3t4(1+t4)3/2
b
1(1+t4)3/2
c
t1+t4
d
231+t4
e
2t3(1+t4)3/2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(3),ddt(3t),ddt(t3)⟩=⟨0,3,3t2⟩‖r′(t)‖=02+(3)2+(3t2)2=9+9t4=9(1+t4)=31+t4

Next, we find the second derivative r″(t): r″(t)=⟨ddt(0),ddt(3),ddt(3t2)⟩=⟨0,0,6t⟩

Now, we compute the cross-product:

r′(t)×r″(t)=⟨0,3,3t2⟩×⟨0,0,6t⟩=|ijk033t2006t|=|33t206t|i−|03t206t|j+|0300|k=18ti

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=|18t|=18t.

Notice that since t>0, we have |t|=t. Therefore, the curvature is

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=18t(31+t4)3=2t3(1+t4)3/2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a General Point
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨3,\,3t,\,{t}^{3}⟩$ for $t>0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩=⟨0,\,3,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(3)^{2}+(3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{9(1+{t}^{4})} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨0,\,3,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\times ⟨0,\,0,\,6t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 6t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 6t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =18t\,i\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =|18t|=18t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$
Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{18t}{{(3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}})}^{3}}=\frac{2t}{3(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

131+t4

t9(1+t4)3/2

decision.explanation: Embedding the curve in three dimensions gives r'(t)=⟨3,-3t²,0⟩ and r''(t)=⟨0,-6t,0⟩. Their cross product has magnitude 18t since t>0, and ‖r'(t)‖=3√(1+t⁴). Therefore κ(t)=18t/[27(1+t⁴)^(3/2)]=2t/[3(1+t⁴)^(3/2)].

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: What is the curvature of the curve $r(t)=⟨3t,1-{t}^{3}⟩$, for $t>0?$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{3})⟩=⟨3,-3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨0,-6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨3,\,-3{t}^{2},\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-6t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & -3{t}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -6t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}3 & -3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & -6t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-18t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=|-18t|=18t.
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{18t}{(3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{18t}{27(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{3(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}

Question 11
?

What is the curvature of the curve r(t)=⟨3t,1−t3⟩, for t>0?

a
6t1+t4
b
t27(1+t4)3/2
c
131+t4
d
t9(1+t4)3/2
e
2t3(1+t4)3/2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ is given by κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(3t),ddt(1−t3)⟩=⟨3,−3t2⟩‖r′(t)‖=32+(−3t2)2=9+9t4=31+t4

Now, we find the second derivative:

r″(t)=⟨ddt(3),ddt(−3t2)⟩=⟨0,−6t⟩

Next, we compute the cross product by considering r′(t) and r″(t) as 3-dimensional vectors with zero z-components:

r′(t)×r″(t)=⟨3,−3t2,0⟩×⟨0,−6t,0⟩=ijk3−3t200−6t0=3−3t20−6tk=−18tk

So, the magnitude of the cross product is ‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=|−18t|=18t. Notice that since t>0, we have |t|=t.

Therefore, the curvature is

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=18t(31+t4)3=18t27(1+t4)3/2=2t3(1+t4)3/2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve
content.problem: What is the curvature of the curve $r(t)=⟨3t,1-{t}^{3}⟩$, for $t>0?$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{3})⟩=⟨3,-3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨0,-6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨3,\,-3{t}^{2},\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-6t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & -3{t}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -6t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}3 & -3{t}^{2} \\ 0 & -6t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-18t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=|-18t|=18t.
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{18t}{(3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{18t}{27(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{3(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of r(t)=⟨1−t2,et⟩ at the point where t=0.

a
2
b
0
c
2

decision.explanation: At t=0, r'(0)=⟨0,1⟩ and r''(0)=⟨-1,1⟩. Adding zero third components, their cross product is ⟨0,0,1⟩, with magnitude 1. Since ‖r'(0)‖=1, the curvature is κ(0)=1/1³=1.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}},\,{e}^{t}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{0}{\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨0,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{(1-{t}^{2})}^{3/2}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-\frac{1}{(1-{0}^{2})^{3/2}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨-1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(0)$ and ${r}^{″}(0)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨0,\,1,0⟩\times ⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}}=\frac{1}{(1)^{3}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t), r′(0), and ‖r′(0)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(1−t2),ddt(et)⟩=⟨−t1−t2,et⟩r′(0)=⟨−01−02,e0⟩=⟨0,1⟩‖r′(0)‖=02+12=1

Now, we find r″(t) and r″(0):

r″(t)=⟨ddt(−t1−t2),ddt(et)⟩=⟨−1(1−t2)3/2,et⟩r″(0)=⟨−1(1−02)3/2,e0⟩=⟨−1,1⟩

Next, we compute the cross product by considering r′(0) and r″(0) as 3-dimensional vectors with zero z-components:

r′(0)×r″(0)=⟨0,1,0⟩×⟨−1,1,0⟩=ijk010−110=01−11k=k‖r′(0)×r″(0)‖=1

Therefore, the curvature at t=0 is

κ(0)=‖r′(0)×r″(0)‖‖r′(0)‖3=1(1)3=1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve
content.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}},\,{e}^{t}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{0}{\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨0,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{(1-{t}^{2})}^{3/2}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-\frac{1}{(1-{0}^{2})^{3/2}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨-1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(0)$ and ${r}^{″}(0)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨0,\,1,0⟩\times ⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}}=\frac{1}{(1)^{3}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

What is the curvature of the curve r(t)=⟨t2,t3⟩, for t>0?

a
6t(4+9t2)3/2
b
6t(4+9t2)1/2
c
6t2(4+9t2)3/2
d
6t(4+9t2)3/2
e
18t(4+9t2)3/2
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2t,3t²⟩ and r''(t)=⟨2,6t⟩. Their cross product has magnitude |12t²−6t²|=6t². Since t>0, ‖r'(t)‖=t√(4+9t²). Therefore κ(t)=6t²/[t³(4+9t²)^(3/2)]=6/[t(4+9t²)^(3/2)].

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩=⟨2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =t\sqrt{4+9{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨2,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,\,3{t}^{2},\,0⟩\times ⟨2,\,6t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 3{t}^{2} & 0 \\ 2 & 6t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 3{t}^{2} \\ 2 & 6t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =6{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=6{t}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}}{(t\sqrt{4+9{t}^{2}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}}{{t}^{3}(4+9{t}^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{t(4+9{t}^{2})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since t>0, we have |t|=t.

Now, we find the second derivative:

r″(t)=⟨ddt(2t),ddt(3t2)⟩=⟨2,6t⟩

Next, we compute the cross product by considering r′(t) and r″(t) as 3-dimensional vectors with zero z-components:

r′(t)×r″(t)=⟨2t,3t2,0⟩×⟨2,6t,0⟩=ijk2t3t2026t0=2t3t226tk=6t2k

So, the magnitude of the cross product is ‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=6t2.

content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩=⟨2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(3{t}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =t\sqrt{4+9{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨2,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,\,3{t}^{2},\,0⟩\times ⟨2,\,6t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 3{t}^{2} & 0 \\ 2 & 6t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 3{t}^{2} \\ 2 & 6t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =6{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=6{t}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}}{(t\sqrt{4+9{t}^{2}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}}{{t}^{3}(4+9{t}^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{t(4+9{t}^{2})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 14
?

Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of r(t)=⟨tcos⁡t,tsin⁡t⟩ as a function of t.

a
t2+2t2+1
b
2t2t2+1
c
t2+2t2+1
d
t2+2(t2+1)3/2
e
t(t2+1)3/2
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨cos t−t sin t, sin t+t cos t⟩ has magnitude √(1+t²). Also r''(t)=⟨−2 sin t−t cos t, 2 cos t−t sin t⟩. The cross product's magnitude is t²+2. Therefore κ(t)=(t²+2)/(t²+1)^(3/2).

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩\times ⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =[(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)]k \\  & =[2{cos}^{2}⁡t-3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t]k \\  & =(2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+{t}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t))k \\  & =({t}^{2}+2)k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖={t}^{2}+2.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{{(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of r(t)=⟨tcos⁡t,tsin⁡t⟩ as a function of t.

a
t2+2t2+1
b
2t2t2+1
c
t2+2t2+1
d
t2+2(t2+1)3/2
e
t(t2+1)3/2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ is given by κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖: r′(t)=⟨ddt(tcos⁡t),ddt(tsin⁡t)⟩=⟨cos⁡t−tsin⁡t,sin⁡t+tcos⁡t⟩‖r′(t)‖=(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)2+(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)2=cos2⁡t−2tsin⁡tcos⁡t+t2sin2⁡t+sin2⁡t+2tsin⁡tcos⁡t+t2cos2⁡t=t2(cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t)+(cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t)=t2+1

Now, we find the second derivative: r″(t)=⟨ddt(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t),ddt(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)⟩=⟨−2sin⁡t−tcos⁡t,2cos⁡t−tsin⁡t⟩

Next, we compute the cross product by considering r′(t) and r″(t) as 3-dimensional vectors with zero z-components: r′(t)×r″(t)=⟨cos⁡t−tsin⁡t,sin⁡t+tcos⁡t,0⟩×⟨−2sin⁡t−tcos⁡t,2cos⁡t−tsin⁡t,0⟩=ijkcos⁡t−tsin⁡tsin⁡t+tcos⁡t0−2sin⁡t−tcos⁡t2cos⁡t−tsin⁡t0=cos⁡t−tsin⁡tsin⁡t+tcos⁡t−2sin⁡t−tcos⁡t2cos⁡t−tsin⁡tk=[(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)(2cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)+(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)(2sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)]k=[2cos2⁡t−3tsin⁡tcos⁡t+t2sin2⁡t+2sin2⁡t+3tsin⁡tcos⁡t+t2cos2⁡t]k=(2(cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t)+t2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t))k=(t2+2)k

So, the magnitude of the cross product is ‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖=t2+2.

Therefore, the curvature is κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3=t2+2(t2+1)3=t2+2(t2+1)3/2.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms ‖r'(t)‖=√(t²+1) and r'(t)×r''(t)=⟨0,0,t²+2⟩. Therefore κ(t)=(t²+2)/(t²+1)^(3/2), confirming option d.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve
content.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩\times ⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =[(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)]k \\  & =[2{cos}^{2}⁡t-3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t]k \\  & =(2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+{t}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t))k \\  & =({t}^{2}+2)k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖={t}^{2}+2.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{{(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of r(t)=⟨t−sin⁡t,1−cos⁡t⟩ at the point where t=π.

a
2
b
4

14

18
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨1−cos t,sin t⟩ and r''(t)=⟨sin t,cos t⟩. At t=π these are ⟨2,0⟩ and ⟨0,−1⟩. Their cross product has magnitude 2, and ‖r'(π)‖=2. Thus κ(π)=2/2³=1/4.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi .$
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨2,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨2,\,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{{2}^{3}}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

The curvature κ(t) is given by

κ(t)=‖r′(t)×r″(t)‖‖r′(t)‖3.

First, we calculate r′(t), r′(π), and ‖r′(π)‖:

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t−sin⁡t),ddt(1−cos⁡t)⟩=⟨1−cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩r′(π)=⟨1−cos⁡π,sin⁡π⟩=⟨2,0⟩‖r′(π)‖=22+02=2

Now, we find r″(t) and r″(π):

r″(t)=⟨ddt(1−cos⁡t),ddt(sin⁡t)⟩=⟨sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩r″(π)=⟨sin⁡π,cos⁡π⟩=⟨0,−1⟩

Next, we compute the cross product by considering r′(π) and r″(π) as 3-dimensional vectors with zero z-components:

r′(π)×r″(π)=⟨2,0,0⟩×⟨0,−1,0⟩=ijk2000−10=200−1k=−2k‖r′(π)×r″(π)‖=2

Therefore, the curvature at t=π is

κ(π)=‖r′(π)×r″(π)‖‖r′(π)‖3=223=14.
